note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Ongoing chest pressure since a couple of hours ago while gardening (light activity, kneeling; not strenuous).
- Character: Diffuse midsternal pressure, “like someone sitting on the chest.”
- Radiation: Pain into left arm and shoulder.
- Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea (no vomiting), feels heart is beating faster now due to stress.
- Timing/progression: Symptoms began a few hours prior to call and are still present at time of consultation.
- Previous episodes: None reported.
- Risk factors/context: Smokes ~10 cigarettes/day for 15 years; hypertension; overweight; low physical activity; family history of premature cardiac disease (father died of heart attack ~age 60; mother with heart problems); alcohol ~7–8 pints of beer/week; cholesterol never checked; denies diabetes.

Past Medical History:
- Hypertension.
- Allergies: Aspirin — allergic reaction with swelling; sometimes mild; no other allergies reported.
- Medications: Not documented (antihypertensive regimen not documented).
- Prior hospitalizations/surgeries: Not documented.
- Family history: Father died of myocardial infarction around age 60; mother with heart problems.
- Social history: Smokes 10 cigarettes/day x15 years; drinks ~7–8 pints beer/week; lives alone; restaurant owner; low physical activity.

Physical Examination:
- Telehealth encounter; no vitals obtained.
- Reported findings: Ongoing chest pressure; pain radiating to left arm/shoulder; shortness of breath; diaphoresis; nausea without vomiting; feels heart beating faster currently.
- Environment/safety: Patient alone at home; front door open for EMS access.

Impression:
- Acute chest pain highly concerning for acute coronary syndrome (possible myocardial infarction).

Management Plan:
- Emergency services activated for immediate evaluation and transport.
- Clinician remained on the line until EMS arrival; instructed patient to keep front door open for access.
- Anticipated EMS actions: Perform ECG and determine appropriate hospital destination and treatment.
- Patient instructed to clearly inform EMS/hospital of aspirin allergy (allergic swelling); aspirin use to be determined by emergency team despite allergy history.
- No medications administered during the call.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with new-onset, persistent midsternal pressure radiating to the left arm/shoulder with dyspnea, diaphoresis, and nausea, raising high concern for ACS. EMS dispatched for urgent ECG and hospital evaluation. Aspirin allergy noted and to be communicated to receiving team.

Key Takeaways:
- Your symptoms may represent a heart attack; EMS is en route for immediate assessment.
- Do not self-take aspirin given your allergy; tell all providers about the swelling reaction.
- Keep the front door open and stay accessible until EMS arrives.

Next Steps:
- EMS to perform ECG and transport to hospital based on findings.
- Hospital-based evaluation and management as per ACS protocol per EMS/hospital team.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vital signs; full medication list and doses; past surgical history; prior cardiac testing/history; pain severity score; cholesterol levels; height/weight/BMI; immunizations; advance directives.
- Internal conflicts: Age/DOB vs stated age (DOB 08/08/1958; clinician estimated ~51; patient said “about sixty”); palpitations statement partly conflicting (“haven’t noticed it beating faster than usual” vs “it’s beating a bit faster now due to stress”) — conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor filler words and a few incomplete sentences but clinically adequate.
